cards.front: How do skeletal muscles exert force on external objects, and how is the human skeleton divided?
cards.back:
Muscles can only pull, not push; they function by pulling against bones that rotate about joint axes, transmitting force through lever systems to manifest external pushing or pulling forces.

The human body contains approximately 206 bones, divided into:
  • Axial Skeleton: Skull (cranium), vertebral column (C1 through coccyx), ribs, and sternum.
  • Appendicular Skeleton: Shoulder/pectoral girdle, pelvic girdle, and bones of the upper and lower extremities.

cards.front: What are the structural regions and respective vertebral counts of the human vertebral column?
cards.back:
The vertebral column consists of 5 anatomical regions separated by flexible intervertebral disks:
  • Cervical vertebrae: 7 (neck region)
  • Thoracic vertebrae: 12 (middle to upper back)
  • Lumbar vertebrae: 5 (lower back)
  • Sacral vertebrae: 5 (fused together; posterior pelvis)
  • Coccygeal vertebrae: 3 to 5 (vestigial internal tail extending downward)

cards.front: How are skeletal joints classified by structural mobility and axes of rotation?
cards.back:
Structural Mobility:
  • Fibrous joints: Virtually no movement (e.g., sutures of the skull).
  • Cartilaginous joints: Limited movement (e.g., intervertebral disks).
  • Synovial joints: Large range of motion with low friction, featuring articulating hyaline cartilage, joint capsules, and synovial fluid (e.g., elbow, knee).
Rotational Axes:
  • Uniaxial: Hinge-like rotation about 1 axis (e.g., elbow; note: knee axis of rotation shifts throughout range of motion).
  • Biaxial: Movement about 2 perpendicular axes (e.g., ankle, wrist).
  • Multiaxial: Movement about all 3 perpendicular spatial axes (e.g., shoulder and hip ball-and-socket joints).

cards.front: What training factors positively stimulate adult skeletal bone mineral density and bone modeling?
cards.back:
Adult bone adapts to muscular force and mechanical loading through:
  • Heavy resistance loading: Elevates bone density and bone mineral content.
  • High-impact explosive movements: Exercises involving hard landings (e.g., gymnastics).
  • Axial skeletal loading: Forces directed along the spine and longitudinal skeletal axis.
  • Frequency and stimulus variation: Because bone adaptation takes substantially longer than skeletal muscle remodeling, stimuli must be systematically varied across frequency, intensity, and modality.

cards.front: Describe the three connective tissue sheaths of skeletal muscle and their role in force transmission.
cards.back:
The body's >430 skeletal muscles are organized by three continuous fibrous connective tissue layers:
  • Epimysium: Outer fibrous layer encasing the entire muscle; contiguous with tendons that attach to bone periosteum.
  • Perimysium: Surrounds bundles (fasciculi) of up to 150 muscle fibers.
  • Endomysium: Encases individual muscle fibers; contiguous with the cell membrane (sarcolemma).
All three sheaths are continuous with the tendon, ensuring tension generated within individual muscle cells transmits directly to the bone.
Anatomical attachments: Proximal (closer to trunk) vs. Distal (farther from trunk) in limbs; Superior (closer to head) vs. Inferior (closer to feet) in the trunk.

cards.front: What constitutes a motor unit, and how does the neuromuscular junction function?
cards.back:
• Neuromuscular Junction (Motor End Plate): The junction between a motor neuron and the muscle fiber it innervates. Each muscle cell possesses only one neuromuscular junction.
  • Motor Unit: A single motor neuron and all the muscle fibers it innervates (ranging from a few to hundreds or thousands of fibers).
  • All-or-None Response: When stimulated by an action potential from the motor neuron, all muscle fibers within that motor unit contract simultaneously.

cards.front: What roles do the sarcoplasmic reticulum and transverse tubules (T-tubules) play in muscle activation?
cards.back:
• Sarcoplasmic Reticulum (SR): An intricate tubular network surrounding each myofibril, terminating as vesicles near the Z-lines that store calcium ions (Ca²⁺).
  • T-Tubules: Run perpendicular to the SR and are contiguous with the sarcolemma at the fiber surface.
  • Coordinated Contraction: Action potentials propagate from the sarcolemma down the T-tubules deep into all levels of the fiber nearly simultaneously, triggering widespread calcium release from the SR vesicles into the myofibril to initiate tension development.

cards.front: Describe the molecular structure of the sarcomere and how its bands change during muscle contraction.
cards.back:
The sarcomere is the smallest contractile unit of skeletal muscle (~2.5 µm resting length), repeated longitudinally across the myofibril:
  • Myosin (thick filaments): ~16 nm diameter, containing ~200 molecules with globular heads that form crossbridges; anchored at the M-bridge in the center of the H-zone.
  • Actin (thin filaments): ~6 nm diameter double helix; anchored at the Z-line.
  • Banding Pattern: A-band corresponds to the alignment of myosin filaments (dark); I-band contains only actin (light), bisected by the Z-line.
  • Contraction Dynamics: Actin slides over myosin toward the center of the sarcomere; the H-zone and I-band shrink, pulling the Z-lines closer together, while the A-band width remains constant.

cards.front: What governs the magnitude of force generated by a muscle at any given instant under the sliding-filament theory?
cards.back:
The actin filaments slide inward on myosin filaments, pulling Z-lines toward the sarcomere center via repetitive flexions of myosin crossbridges.

Primary Force Principle: The amount of force produced by a muscle at any instant in time is directly related to the number of myosin crossbridges bound to actin filaments cross-sectionally at that exact instant.

cards.front: Outline the five sequential phases of muscular contraction and relaxation.
cards.back:
1. Resting Phase: Minimal calcium in myofibril; actin sites covered; weak actin–myosin interaction without tension.
  2. Excitation–Contraction Coupling: Action potential triggers SR calcium release; Ca²⁺ binds to troponin, causing a shift in tropomyosin to expose active binding sites on actin for rapid crossbridge attachment.
  3. Contraction Phase: Hydrolysis of ATP to ADP and inorganic phosphate (catalyzed by myosin ATPase) powers the crossbridge pull (power stroke). A fresh ATP binds to detach the myosin head.
  4. Recharge Phase: Repeated cycles of binding, power stroke, detachment, and recocking continue as long as Ca²⁺, ATP, and active myosin ATPase remain available.
  5. Relaxation Phase: Motor nerve stimulation ceases; calcium is actively pumped back into the SR, tropomyosin covers actin sites, and filaments return to their unbound state.
